Empirical Research Plan: 2006 – 2008 Massachusetts Health‐Care Reform

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────
Preferred strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension.

Why appropriate?
• The reform was a discrete, well-timed, statewide shock that dramatically increased insurance coverage starting mid-2006 and fully phased-in by 2007.  
• The claims data give repeated observations on the same individuals before and after the law.  
• A credible comparison group is available: residents of other New-England states (RI, CT, NH, ME, VT) whose health-care environment and business cycle conditions are similar but who did not face the reform.  
• DID leverages the panel structure, nets out common time shocks, and isolates the reform’s causal effect on utilization.

We will complement DID with an event-study (dynamic leads/lags) to inspect pre-trends and the time path of effects.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable
• Treated = 1 for individuals residing in Massachusetts (MA).  
• Treated = 0 for individuals residing in comparison states (New England minus MA).

Treatment timing
• Event date t0 = 2006 Q3 (date the mandate and subsidized exchange were enacted).  
• Pre-period: 2005 Q1 – 2006 Q2 (4 quarters)  
• Post-period: 2007 Q1 – 2008 Q4 (8 quarters)  
• We drop the implementation/transition quarters 2006 Q3–Q4 to avoid contamination.

Outcome variables
(1) ln(HospitalAdmissions_it)  
(2) ln(PreventiveVisits_it)  
Alternative: indicator for any admission / any preventive visit.

Control group (counterfactual)
• Residents of RI, CT, NH, ME, VT in the same database.  
• Rationale: geographically close, similar provider market structure, no contemporaneous insurance expansion.

Sub-samples for heterogeneity
• Low-income ZIP codes vs. high-income ZIPs (triple-diff)  
• Previously uninsured vs. continuously insured individuals (needs historical eligibility flags)

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of the MA reform, utilization trends in MA would have followed those in the comparison states.  
  Plausibility: New-England states experienced similar macro conditions. Pre-period event-study coefficients allow testing.

A2. Stable composition: No differential migration or differential data reporting across states that is correlated with the reform.  
  Plausibility: Short horizon (3 yrs) and limited inter-state migration in New England.

A3. No policy spillovers / interference: Massachusetts reform did not affect utilization behavior of residents in the control states.  
  Plausibility: Health-insurance markets are regulated at the state level; little cross-state insurance purchase.

A4. Common shocks properly controlled: National events (e.g., Great Recession onset in 2008) hit both groups similarly; quarter fixed effects absorb them.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Differential recession impact (2007–08).  
  • Mitigation: State-specific linear time trends; county-level unemployment controls; robustness dropping 2008Q3–Q4.

T2. Spillovers through cross-border care (RI residents using MA hospitals, etc.).  
  • Mitigation: Assign treatment by residence ZIP rather than hospital location; re-estimate excluding border counties.

T3. Pre-existing policy differences (e.g., Medicaid eligibility rules).  
  • Mitigation: Include state-by-year Medicaid enrollment rates as controls; triple-diff with low-income ZIP codes whose Medicaid expansions were comparable.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)    # fast I/O
library(fixest)        # high-dim FE regressions
library(ggplot2)       # plots

# 1. Load & merge -----------------------------------------------------------
claims <- fread("all_payer_claims_2005_2008.csv")   # hypothetical file

# 2. Core variable construction --------------------------------------------
# Restrict to adults 19–64
claims <- claims[age >= 19 & age <= 64]

# State of residence
claims[, treat := as.integer(state == "MA")]

# Calendar quarter
claims[, quarter := as.yearqtr(service_date)]

# Drop transition quarters
claims <- claims[!(quarter %in% c("2006 Q3","2006 Q4"))]

# Pre/Post indicator
claims[, post := as.integer(quarter >= "2007 Q1")]

# Outcomes
claims[, hosp_any := as.integer(hospital_adm > 0)]
claims[, prev_any := as.integer(preventive_visits > 0)]
claims[, ln_adm  := log1p(hospital_adm)]
claims[, ln_prev := log1p(preventive_visits)]

# 3. Main DID specification -------------------------------------------------
did_spec <- feols(ln_adm ~ treat*post | id + quarter,
                  data = claims, cluster = ~state)

summary(did_spec)

# 4. Event Study (leads/lags) ----------------------------------------------
# Define event-time variable relative to 2007Q1
claims[, rel_qtr := as.integer(quarter) - as.integer(as.yearqtr("2007 Q1"))]

# Interact treat with each rel_qtr
event_spec <- feols(ln_adm ~ i(rel_qtr, treat, ref = -1) | id + quarter,
                    data = claims, cluster = ~state)

iplot(event_spec)      # built-in plotting of coefficients

# 5. Robustness: Border counties dropped -----------------------------------
claims_border <- claims[county %in% border_counties == FALSE]

robust_did <- feols(ln_adm ~ treat*post | id + quarter,
                    data = claims_border, cluster = ~state)

etable(did_spec, robust_did, dict = c(`treat:post` = "MA Reform Effect"))
```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────
Economic theory predicts:
• More insurance reduces out-of-pocket price, raising demand for non-emergency care; some offset from better preventive care may reduce avoidable hospitalizations.

Priors:
a. Preventive visits: +10 – 20 %.  
b. Hospital admissions: net effect ambiguous; short run slight increase (5 %) due to newly found conditions, longer-run small decline for ACS (ambulatory-care-sensitive) admissions.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
────────────────────────────────────────
C1: Pre-trend similarity visually and statistically checked …… 1  
C2: No anticipatory behavior (drop transition, inspect leads) … 1  
C3: No interference / spillovers across units …………………… 0.5  
C4: Stable sample composition (no selective migration) ……… 0.5  
C5: Correct functional form & clustering …………………………… 1  
Total (max 5) = 4.0 → reasonably strong design.

────────────────────────────────────────
End of plan
